title: Product (business)
content:
In marketing and economics, a product is any object, service, or system offered to a market to satisfy a customer’s need or want. Products may be tangible, such as physical goods that can be touched and owned, or intangible, such as services, digital offerings, or rights that provide value without physical form. Products are created through processes of design, production, and distribution, and they play a central role in commercial exchange, consumer behavior, and organizational strategy. [...] Beyond marketing, the term product is also used in fields such as manufacturing, where it refers to finished goods derived from raw materials, and project management, where it denotes deliverables produced to achieve defined objectives. Because products directly affect consumer safety, economic activity, and environmental sustainability, they are often subject to regulation, classification systems, and information-disclosure requirements across different jurisdictions.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Anything that can be offered to a market

For other uses, see [Product](/wiki/Product_(disambiguation) "Product (disambiguation)").

In **marketing and economics**, a **product** is any object, service, or system offered to a market to satisfy a customer’s need or want. Products may be **tangible**, such as physical goods that can be touched and owned, or **intangible**, such as services, digital offerings, or rights that provide value without physical form. Products are created through processes of design, production, and distribution, and they play a central role in commercial exchange, consumer behavior, and organizational strategy.

Beyond marketing, the term *product* is also used in fields such as **manufacturing**, where it refers to finished goods derived from raw materials, and **project management**, where it denotes deliverables produced to achieve defined objectives.[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1) Because products directly affect consumer safety, economic activity, and environmental sustainability, they are often subject to **regulation, classification systems, and information-disclosure requirements** across different jurisdictions.

## Product classification

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Product classification")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Eurail_Pass_and_Guide.jpg/250px-Eurail_Pass_and_Guide.jpg)](/wiki/File:Eurail_Pass_and_Guide.jpg)

Eurail, a type of rail pass for multiple journeys by train, an intangible product

A product can be classified as [tangible](/wiki/Tangible_asset "Tangible asset") or [intangible](/wiki/Intangible_asset "Intangible asset"). A tangible product is an actual physical object that can be perceived by touch, such as a building, vehicle, gadget, or clothing. An intangible product is a product that can only be perceived indirectly, such as an insurance policy. These [services](/wiki/Service_(economics) "Service (economics)") can be broadly classified under intangible products, which can be [durable or nondurable](/wiki/Durable_goods "Durable goods").

### By use

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: By use")]

In its online product catalog, retailer [Sears, Roebuck and Company](/wiki/Sears,_Roebuck_and_Company "Sears, Roebuck and Company") divides its products into "departments", then presents products to potential shoppers according to (1) function or (2) brand. Each product has a Sears item number and a manufacturer's model number. Sears uses the departments and product groupings with the intention of helping customers browse products by function or brand within a traditional [department-store](/wiki/Department_store "Department store") structure.[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1)

### By association

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: By association")]

A [product line](/wiki/Product_line "Product line") is "a group of products which are closely related, either because they function similarly, are sold to the same customer groups, are marketed through the same types of outlets, or fall within given price ranges".[[2]](#cite_note-2) Many businesses offer a range of product lines (their "product mix") which may be unique to a single organisation or may be common across the business's industry. Within the [insurance](/wiki/Insurance "Insurance") industry, product lines are indicated by the type of risk coverage, such as [auto insurance](/wiki/Auto_insurance "Auto insurance"), commercial [insurance](/wiki/Insurance "Insurance"), and [life insurance](/wiki/Life_insurance "Life insurance").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Companies such as [Pepsi](/wiki/Pepsi "Pepsi") and [Coca-Cola](/wiki/Coca-Cola "Coca-Cola") are considered to have a very large and diverse product mix.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) Some companies use a large product mix to reach a number of market segments.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In 2002 the [US Census](/wiki/US_Census "US Census") compiled revenue figures for the finance and insurance industry by various product lines such as "accident, health and medical insurance premiums" and "income from secured consumer loans".[[6]](#cite_note-6)

### National and international product classifications

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: National and international product classifications")]

Various classification systems for products have been developed for economic statistical purposes. The NAFTA signatories are working on a system that classifies products called NAPCS as a companion to the [North American Industry Classification System](/wiki/North_American_Industry_Classification_System "North American Industry Classification System") (NAICS).[[7]](#cite_note-7) The European Union uses a "Classification of Products by Activity" among other product classifications.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The United Nations also classifies products for international economic activity reporting.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The **Aspinwall Classification System** [[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) classifies and rates products based on five variables:

1. Replacement rate (How frequently is the product repurchased?)
2. Gross margin (How much profit is obtained from each product?)
3. Buyer goal adjustment (How flexible are the buyers' purchasing habits about this product?)
4. Duration of product satisfaction (How long will the product produce benefits for the user?)
5. Duration of buyer search behavior (How long will consumers shop for the product?)

The National Institute of Governmental Purchasing (NIGP)[[12]](#cite_note-12) developed a commodity and services classification system for use by state and local governments, the [NIGP Code](/wiki/NIGP_Code "NIGP Code").[[13]](#cite_note-13) The NIGP Code is used by 33 states within the United States as well as thousands of cities, counties, and political subdivisions. The NIGP Code is a hierarchical schema consisting of a 3-digit class, 5-digit class-item, 7-digit class-item-group, and an 11-digit class-item-group-detail.[[14]](#cite_note-14) Applications of the NIGP Code include vendor registration, inventory item identification, contract item management, spend analysis, and strategic sourcing.

## Product model

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Product model")]

A manufacturer usually provides an identifier for each particular design of product they make, known as a **model**, **model variant**, or **model number** (often abbreviated as **MN**, **M/N** or **model no.**, and sometimes as [M- or Mk](/wiki/Mark_(designation) "Mark (designation)")). For example, [Dyson Ltd](/wiki/Dyson_(company) "Dyson (company)"), a manufacturer of appliances (mainly vacuum cleaners), requires customers to identify their model in the support section of the website.[[15]](#cite_note-15) [Brand](/wiki/Brand "Brand") and model can be used together to identify products in the market. The model number is not necessarily the same as the [manufacturer part number](/wiki/Manufacturer_part_number "Manufacturer part number") (MPN).[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Because of the huge amount of similar products in the [automotive industry](/wiki/Automotive_industry "Automotive industry"), there is a special kind of defining a car with options (marks, attributes) that represent the characteristics of the vehicle. A model of a car is defined by some basic options like body, engine, gearbox, and axles. The variants of a model (often called the **trim levels**) are built with some additional options like color, seats, wheels, mirrors, other trims, entertainment, and assistant systems, etc. Options that exclude each other (pairwise) build an option family. That means that you can choose only one option for each family, and you have to choose exactly one option.

In addition, a specific unit of a product is often (and in some contexts must be) identified by a [serial number](/wiki/Serial_number "Serial number"), which is necessary to distinguish products with the same product definition. In the case of automotive products, it is called the [vehicle identification number](/wiki/Vehicle_identification_number "Vehicle identification number") (VIN), an internationally standardised format.

## Product information

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Product information")]

See also: [Product analysis](/wiki/Product_analysis "Product analysis")

Product information, beyond [currency](/wiki/Currency "Currency") price information, can include:[[17]](#cite_note-978-0-262-03492-0-17)[*[additional citation(s) needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

* Product description – typically on a label on or [packaging](/wiki/Packaging "Packaging") of the product or in [an online shopping website for it](/wiki/Online_shopping#Product_selection "Online shopping")
* [Certificates](/wiki/Product_certification "Product certification") – including [related to sustainability](/wiki/Sustainability_standards_and_certification "Sustainability standards and certification") and for unobservable quality attributes[[18]](#cite_note-18)
* Various types of ratings, comparisons, third-party information, and [customer reviews](/wiki/Customer_review "Customer review") – including [user reviews](/wiki/User_review "User review")
* [Labels](/wiki/Label "Label")[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) – such as [energy rating labels](/wiki/Energy_rating_label "Energy rating label")
* Information about ingredients
* Visual content
* Place/region and company of origin
* Estimated [expiration date](/wiki/Expiration_date "Expiration date")
* Safety information
* Nutrition information, mainly contained [macronutrients](/wiki/Macronutrients "Macronutrients")

Many of these types of product information are regulated to some degree, such as to some degree prohibiting false or misleading product information or requiring sellers or manufacturers to specify various information, such as ingredients of food, pharmaceutical, and hygiene products. There is also [standardization](/wiki/Standardization "Standardization"). Marketing to entice the shopper[[17]](#cite_note-978-0-262-03492-0-17) is often prioritized over accurate, high-quality, or extensive and relevant information.

Product information is often a key element in the [buyer decision process](/wiki/Buyer_decision_process "Buyer decision process"). Relevant factors include trust in the accuracy of the information and social normative pressure.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) Easily accessible and up-to-date medicinal product information can contribute to the [health literacy](/wiki/Health_literacy "Health literacy").[[24]](#cite_note-24) Online shopping is usually more informationally rich than shopping at physical stores, traveled to, and usually has higher comparability and customizability.[[17]](#cite_note-978-0-262-03492-0-17)

Production information-related developments can be useful for enabling, facilitating, or shifting towards [sustainable consumption](/wiki/Sustainable_consumption "Sustainable consumption") and supporting more [sustainable productss](/wiki/Sustainable_products "Sustainable products"). Environmental [life-cycle assessment](/wiki/Life-cycle_assessment "Life-cycle assessment") (LCA) has been widely used to assess environmental impacts across the life cycle of products.[[25]](#cite_note-25) There are [LCA datasets](/wiki/Life-cycle_assessment#LCA_dataset_creation "Life-cycle assessment") that assess all products in some supermarkets in a standardized way.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) Consumers may seek reliable [information to evaluate](/wiki/Data-informed_decision-making "Data-informed decision-making") relevant characteristics of products such as durability and reliability.[[28]](#cite_note-28) Development of 'transparency by design' scenarios have been suggested to "complement the physical product with layers of digital information", improving transparency and traceability (T&T).[[29]](#cite_note-29) The app CodeCheck gives some smartphone users some capability to scan products for assessed ingredients.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31) Many labels are considered to be flawed and few have the time to "study the true environmental impact of every purchase". Full product transparency is a concept of making the full life-cycle impacts public.[[32]](#cite_note-32) An important element that is required for various product information is [supply chain](/wiki/Supply_chain "Supply chain") transparency, which relates to human rights and [supply chain sustainability](/wiki/Supply_chain_sustainability "Supply chain sustainability").[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)

### Produce traceability

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Produce traceability")]

This section is an excerpt from [Produce traceability](/wiki/Produce_traceability "Produce traceability").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Produce_traceability&action=edit)]

[Produce traceability](/wiki/Produce_traceability "Produce traceability") makes it possible to track produce from its point of origin to a retail location where it is purchased by consumers.

Produce [traceability](/wiki/Traceability "Traceability") is an important link in protecting public health since it allows health agencies to more quickly and accurately identify the source of [contaminated](/wiki/Contamination "Contamination") fruit or vegetables believed to be the cause of an [outbreak](/wiki/Outbreak "Outbreak") of [foodborne illness](/wiki/Foodborne_illness "Foodborne illness"), remove them from the marketplace, and communicate to the supply chain.

### Product passports

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Product passports")]

In the EU, under the renewed [Sustainable Product Policy Initiative](/wiki/Sustainable_Product_Policy_Initiative "Sustainable Product Policy Initiative"), the inclusion of a [Digital Product Passport](/wiki/Digital_Product_Passport "Digital Product Passport") has been proposed.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36) A [material passport](/wiki/Material_passport "Material passport") is a document consisting of all the materials that are included in a product or construction. It consists of a set of data describing defined characteristics of materials in products, useful for recovery, [recycling](/wiki/Recycling "Recycling"), re-use, and various evaluations. They may contribute to a more [circular economy](/wiki/Circular_economy "Circular economy").

### Product information management

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Product_(business)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Product information management")]

This section is an excerpt from [Product information management](/wiki/Product_information_management "Product information management").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Product_information_management&action=edit)]

[Product information management](/wiki/Product_information_management "Product information management") (PIM) is the process of [managing](/wiki/Data_management "Data management") all the information required to market and sell products through [distribution channels](/wiki/Distribution_channel "Distribution channel"). This product data is created by an internal organization to support a [multichannel marketing](/wiki/Multichannel_marketing "Multichannel marketing") strategy. A central hub of product data can be used to distribute information to sales channels such as [e-commerce](/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") websites, print catalogues, marketplaces such as [Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") and [Google Shopping](/wiki/Google_Shopping "Google Shopping"), social media platforms like [Instagram](/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") and electronic [data feeds](/wiki/Data_feed "Data feed") to trading partners. Moreover, the significant role that PIM plays is reducing the [abandonment rate](/wiki/Abandonment_rate "Abandonment rate") by giving better product information.[[37]](#cite_note-37)
